doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Why he avoided studio work and conducting under overtime culture
summary: Gibbs says he wants control of his musical department and disliked studio dates padded for overtime pay.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: No, no. Only from the band. You know something? When I worked with Steve Allen for years, conducting, my job was to conduct. There’s a director and a producer. Whatever they have to tell me. But if it comes to my department, they hire me to do the job, I’ll tell them. Otherwise don’t give me that job. And I’ll take a lot of advice of musicians. The thing is, but I don’t do record — when I first moved to California I’d go to do a record date and there’d be some idiot up there and we’d be doing 84 takes and I’d want to say, “Make that an E flat and that would solve the problem, we could go straight ahead.” But you can’t do that because everybody wants to make overtime money. It’s a business. You know they want — they’d stay there twenty hours because it gets to a certain time, double money. I couldn’t stand there, so I never would do studio work because of that. The music would be — I didn’t care how good or bad it was because there was always good musicians playing it. It’s just that sometimes the band leader, he didn’t know, because the guy that writes the arrangements sometimes, they’re not band leaders, they’re © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

good arrangers, and sometimes when it came to the rock era, there’d be no music, they didn’t even know what they’re doing. You get a lead sheet, and you have to make up your own part half the time. But then again you’d stay there hours because it’s an E flat chord. If he would just say “E flat” and we all played it, that would solve the whole problem. But he’d mention everything but E flat. And the guys loved it because they’d go home with a lot of money. And that wasn’t for me. The music has always been the most important thing.
